doc.title: Rick Margitza interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 22, 2024

title: Playing outside the changes and the Intervallic Families method
summary: He explains 365 Days of Practice and Gary Campbell's method of dividing the octave to justify a C sharp over A minor.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: The reason I said that so quickly is because —

I was looking at them and there’s things in there in many of your solos that from a harmonic standpoint are breaking the tonality. I’m going to use that term because you used it. For instance the chord symbol is A minor and you’re playing a C sharp. So I’m trying to figure out, I don’t have a question here but this idea of playing outside the change has fascinated me. It’s something I have trouble doing myself. Is, in your head is there a theory behind that or — I did notice that a lot of times when you’re playing outside the change it’s part of a sequence you’re doing. You’ve got a phrase and you’re going to repeat it but you’re going to move up or down even though let’s say the chord may not go with that. I don’t know what you can do with that comment, but —

Yeah. Well I’m not sure if — you talked about having notes for what we’re going to talk about — I have a book that came out last — in January. If that’s going to be part of what we’re going to talk about.
Yeah I’d like to get to that 365 Days.

So in that book — so we could talk about the structure of the book later but in the beginning of that book I talk about this practice routine that I kind of learned and developed as a result of studying with a great saxophone player named Gary Campbell who was teaching at the University of Miami when I was there some years ago, and who also went to Indiana University when Michael Brecker was there so they used to practice together. And Michael always credits Gary as being a big influence on his practicing. So this is all a preface to answering your question. Part of this practice method is a thing called the “Intervallic Families” and it comes from dividing up the octave. So there’s half steps, whole steps, minor thirds, major thirds, fourths, tritones, and fifths. And after fifths any interval bigger than that could be — what’s the word — reverted back to one of the other intervals. So say for example a minor sixth, from C to A flat is just an inversion of a major third, from A flat to C. And in a major sixth, from C to A is just an inversion of a minor third. So basically you have half steps, whole steps, minor thirds, major thirds, fourths and fifths. So if you memorize those groups then you start seeing how you can get from any note in any key over any chord. So say for example you say A minor and then you say C sharp. So if you think about A minor moving up in major thirds, so that gives you A minor, C sharp minor, and F minor. So we’re thinking about A is the root, and moving up in major thirds. Right? So A minor, C sharp minor, F minor. So that C sharp, although against an A chord, it’s the major third, but it’s the root of C sharp minor. So if you play — something goes from C sharp minor down to A minor, or you can go up, C sharp minor, F minor to A minor, the parallel nature of what you’re playing justifies that wrong sound.
Or yeah. I call it justifying it or neutralizing it.
In your head, let’s see, I’m trying to phrase this, what is the — where does the part come in, does it sound good? After all that pausing that was a heck of an adjective.

Well two things. You asked the question earlier about a system and structures and patterns. That’s the dangerous thing about practicing this way is you don’t want to sound too mechanical and sound like you’re playing too many patterns. So you have to practice patterns to not be afraid of that C sharp over A minor because you know how to get back to where you need to be. And then slowly but surely when you practice this way it just becomes a natural way of hearing music as opposed to — so to me you want to be able to kind of really combine the brain and the heart and the ears. So the brain comes in when you’re studying the theory and practicing all the patterns. And then the ears come is like when I hear an A minor on the piano I hear that C sharp now as part of the — it’s a totally acceptable note to use. It’s not anything to be afraid of because I know how to relate it back to the A minor. I lost your voice.
